title: Of experience
paragraphs: There is no desire more natural than the desire for knowledge. We try every road that may lead us to it; where reason falls short, we call in experience,
"Per varios usus artem experientia fecit, Exemplo monstrante viam,"
["By various trials experience created art, example showing the way." — Manilius, i. 59.]

which is a much weaker and cheaper instrument; but truth is so great a thing that we ought not to disdain any mediation that will guide us to it. Reason has so many forms that we hardly know which one to take; experience has no fewer; the inference we would draw from comparing events is shaky, since events are never alike. There is no quality so universal in this picture of things as diversity and variety. Greeks, Latins, and we ourselves use eggs as the standard example of resemblance — and yet there have been men, one in particular at Delphi, who could tell so many marks of difference among eggs that he never mistook one for another, and with a yard full of hens could say which had laid which.

Dissimilarity intrudes by itself into our own work; no craft can reach perfect resemblance. Neither Perrozet nor any other can polish and bleach the backs of his cards so carefully that some gamblers will not pick them out by simply seeing them shuffled by someone else. Likeness does not so much make one thing as difference makes another. Nature has committed herself to making nothing that was not unlike something else.

And yet I am not much pleased with the opinion of the man who thought to curb the authority of judges by multiplying laws and cutting out their portions for them; he failed to see that there is as much liberty and latitude in the interpretation of laws as in their composition. People only fool themselves who imagine they can damp down our disputes by recalling us to the express words of the Bible; for our minds find no narrower field for contesting another's meaning than for setting out their own — as if there were less animosity and tartness in commentary than in invention. We see how mistaken he was, for we have more laws in France than the rest of the world put together, and more than would be needed to govern all the worlds of Epicurus:
"Ut olim flagitiis, sic nunc legibus, laboramus."
["As we were once burdened by crimes, so now we are overburdened by laws." — Tacitus, Annals, iii. 25.]

And yet we have left so much to the opinions and decisions of our judges that there has never been so full a liberty, or so full a licence. What have our legislators gained by picking out a hundred thousand particular cases and applying to them a hundred thousand laws? The number bears no proportion to the infinite diversity of human action; multiplying our inventions will never catch up with the variety of examples. Add a hundred times as many more, and still it will not happen that any of the events to come will tally with any of these millions of recorded events, or be so exactly coupled and matched with one that no circumstance and no difference remain to require a different judgment. There is little relation between our actions, which are in perpetual change, and fixed unchanging laws. The most desirable laws are the rarest, simplest, and most general; and I am even of the opinion that we would be better off with none at all than with the staggering number we have.

Nature always gives them better and happier than the ones we make ourselves; witness the picture of the Golden Age in the poets, and the state in which we see those nations live who have no other. Some there are who, for their only judge, take the first passer-by who walks along their mountains, to settle their case; and others who, on market day, pick someone on the spot from among them to decide their quarrels. What danger would there be in having the wisest among us settle ours that way, by the case in front of him and on the spot, without obligation of precedent or consequence? Every foot its own shoe. King Ferdinand, sending colonies to the Indies, wisely arranged that they should not carry with them any students of jurisprudence, for fear lawsuits should get a foothold in that new world — a science that by its very nature breeds quarrel and division — agreeing with Plato that "lawyers and physicians are bad institutions for a country."

How is it that our common language, so easy for every other purpose, turns obscure and unintelligible in wills and contracts? Why is it that the man who expresses himself clearly in everything else he says or writes cannot find in these any way of declaring himself that does not fall into doubt and contradiction? Is it not that the princes of that art, applying themselves with peculiar attention to picking out portentous words and contriving artificial sentences, have so weighed every syllable and so thoroughly sifted every sort of quirking connection that they are now confounded and tangled in the infinity of figures and minute divisions, and can no longer fall under any rule, any prescription, or any certain understanding?
"Confusum est, quidquid usque in pulverem sectum est."
["Whatever is beaten into powder is indistinguishable." — Seneca, Epist., 89.]

Watch children trying to push a mass of quicksilver into a certain number of parts: the more they press and work it and try to bend it to their will, the more they irritate the liberty of this generous metal; it escapes their efforts and sprinkles itself into so many separate bodies that all reckoning is defeated. So it is here: in subdividing these subtleties we teach men to multiply their doubts; they put us in the way of stretching and varying difficulties, lengthening and dispersing them. By sowing and retailing questions they make the world fruitful and luxuriant in uncertainties and disputes, as the earth is made fertile by being broken up and dug deep.
"Difficultatem facit doctrina."
["Doctrine begets difficulty." — Quintilian, Inst. Orat., x. 3.]

We doubted Ulpian, and now we are still more perplexed by Bartolus and Baldus. We should be wiping out the trace of this innumerable diversity of opinions, not decking ourselves with it and filling posterity with quibbles. I don't know what to say to it; but experience makes it plain that so many interpretations dissipate truth and break it up. Aristotle wrote to be understood; if he could not manage it, another writer who is not as good at it will manage even less, and a third, copying his own thoughts onto Aristotle's, less still. We crack open the matter, and spill it in the pouring out; out of one subject we make a thousand, and in multiplying and subdividing them fall again into the infinity of atoms of Epicurus. No two men ever made the same judgment of the same thing; it is impossible to find two opinions exactly alike, not only in different men but in the same man at different hours. I often find matter of doubt in things the commentary has disdained to notice; I am most apt to stumble on level ground, like certain horses I have known that trip most on the smoothest road.

Who will deny that glosses augment doubts and ignorance, since no book is to be found, human or divine, that the world busies itself with, whose difficulties have been cleared up by interpretation? The hundredth commentator hands it on to the next, still more knotty and tangled than he found it. When were we ever agreed among ourselves: "This book has enough; there is no more to be said about it"? This is most apparent in the law; we give the authority of law to infinite doctors, infinite decrees, and as many interpretations — and do we find any end to the need of interpreting? Is there, for all that, any progress toward peace, or do we stand in need of any fewer advocates and judges than when this great mass of law was still in its infancy? On the contrary, we darken and bury understanding; we can no longer find it except at the mercy of so many fences and barriers. Men do not know the natural disease of the mind; it does nothing but ferret and inquire, and is forever wheeling, juggling, perplexing itself like silkworms, and then smothers itself in its own work: "Mus in pice." It thinks it sees, at a great distance, I know not what glimpses of light and imaginary truth; but as it runs toward them, so many difficulties, obstacles, and new inquiries cross its path that it loses its way and is made drunk with the motion — not unlike Aesop's dogs, who, seeing something like a dead body floating in the sea and not being able to reach it, set about drinking the water dry to lay the passage open, and so choked themselves. To this, what Crates said of the writings of Heraclitus fits well enough: "that they required a reader who could swim well," so the depth and weight of his learning would not overwhelm and stifle him. It is nothing but particular weakness that makes us content with what others or we ourselves have found in this chase after knowledge; a better understanding will not rest there. There is always room for one to follow — even for ourselves — and another road; our inquiries have no end; our end is in the other world. It is a sign either that the mind has grown short-sighted when it is satisfied, or that it has grown tired. No generous mind can stop within itself; it always strains further, and beyond its power; it has sallies beyond its effects; if it does not advance and press forward, retire and rush and wheel about, it is only half alive. Its pursuits have no boundary and no method; its food is wonder, the chase, ambiguity, which Apollo plainly enough declared by always speaking to us in a double, obscure, and oblique sense — not feeding us but amusing and puzzling us. It is an irregular and perpetual motion, without model and without aim; its inventions warm, chase, and breed one another:
Estienne de la Boétie; thus translated by Cotton:

"So in a running stream one wave we see / After another roll incessantly, / And as they glide, each does successively / Pursue the other, each the other fly / By this that's evermore pushed on, and this / By that continually preceded is: / The water still does into water swill, / Still the same brook, but different water still."

There is more trouble in interpreting interpretations than in interpreting things, and more books written about books than about any other subject; we do nothing but comment on one another. Every place swarms with commentaries; of original authors there is a great shortage. Is it not the chief and most respected knowledge of our later ages to understand the learned? Is it not the common and final aim of all studies? Our opinions are grafted onto one another; the first serves as stock for the second, the second for the third, and so on; step by step we climb the ladder; and so the one who has mounted highest has often more honour than merit, for he is only an inch higher than the next, on the next man's shoulders.

How often, and perhaps how foolishly, I have stretched my book to make it speak of itself; foolishly, if for no other reason than this, that it should remind me of what I say about others who do the same — that the frequent amorous glances they cast at their own work testify that their hearts pant with self-love, and that even the disdainful severity with which they scourge their writings is only the dandling and caressing of maternal love. As with Aristotle, whose praise and dispraise of himself often spring from the same air of arrogance. My own excuse is that on this matter I ought to have more liberty than others, since I am writing specifically about myself and my writings, as I do about my other actions; that my theme turns on itself. But I'm not sure others will accept this excuse.

I noticed in Germany that Luther has left as many divisions and disputes about the doubt in his own opinions, and more, as he raised over Holy Scripture. Our contest is verbal. I ask what nature is, what pleasure, what "circle" and "substitution" are; the question is about words, and is answered in the same way. "A stone is a body." But if a man should go on: "And what is a body?" — "Substance." "And what is substance?" and so on, he would drive the respondent to the end of his Calepin.
[Calepin (Ambrogio da Calepio), a famous lexicographer of the fifteenth century. His Polyglot Dictionary became so famous that "Calepin" became a common term for a lexicon.]

We exchange one word for another, and often for one less understood. I know better what "man" is than I know what "Animal," "Mortal," or "Rational" is. To answer one doubt, they hand me three; it is the Hydra's head. Socrates asked Meno, "What is virtue?" — "There is," says Meno, "the virtue of a man and of a woman, of a magistrate and of a private person, of an old man and of a child." — "Very fine," cried Socrates, "we were looking for one virtue, and you have brought us a whole swarm." We put one question, and they return a whole hive. As no event and no face entirely resembles another, neither does it entirely differ: an ingenious mixture by nature. If our faces were not alike, we could not tell man from beast; if they were not unlike, we could not tell one man from another. All things hold together by some resemblance; every example limps; and the relation drawn from experience is always faulty and imperfect. Comparisons are always coupled at one end or the other; and so do laws serve, fitted to each of our affairs by some wrenched, biased, and forced interpretation.

Since the ethical laws, which concern only each person's particular duty to himself, are so hard to frame, as we see they are, it is no wonder if those that govern so many particulars are even harder. Look at the shape of the justice that governs us; it is a true testimony to human weakness, so full it is of error and contradiction. What we find to be favour or severity in justice — and we find so much of both, that I doubt the middle ground is even reached as often — are sickly and unjust members of the very body and essence of justice. Some country people have just brought me news in great haste that they had left in a forest of mine a man with a hundred wounds on him, still breathing, who begged them for water out of pity and for help to carry him to some place of shelter. They tell me they didn't dare go near him, for fear that the officers of justice should find them with him and, as happens to those discovered near a murdered person, they would be called to answer for the death, to their utter ruin, having neither money nor friends to defend their innocence. What could I have said to those people? It is certain that this office of humanity would have brought them to grief.

How many innocent people we have known who have been punished — and this without any fault of the judge; and how many that have never come to our knowledge? This happened in my time: certain men had been condemned to die for a murder; their sentence was, if not pronounced, at least decided and settled on. The judges, just at that moment, are informed by the officers of a lower court nearby that they have some men in custody who have plainly confessed to the murder and given an indubitable account of all the particulars of the deed. Yet it was gravely debated whether they ought to suspend the execution of the sentence already passed on the first accused. They weighed the novelty of the example judicially, and the consequence of reversing judgments — that the sentence had been passed, and the judges were therefore deprived of repentance — and in the result these poor wretches were sacrificed by the forms of justice. Philip, or someone, guarded against a similar problem afterward in this way. He had condemned a man to a heavy fine in favour of another by a final judgment. The truth coming out some time later, he found that he had passed an unjust sentence. On the one side stood the merits of the cause, on the other the principles of judicial form; he satisfied both in a way, leaving the sentence standing and compensating the wronged party out of his own purse. But he had to do with a reparable affair; my men were irreparably hanged. How many condemnations have I seen more criminal than the crimes themselves?

All of which makes me remember the ancient opinions: "That a man must necessarily do wrong by retail who wants to do right wholesale, and do injustice in little things to do justice in big ones; that human justice is formed after the model of medicine, by which everything useful is also just and honest"; and the Stoic view that nature herself proceeds contrary to justice in most of her works; and the Cyrenaic view that nothing is just of itself, but custom and laws make justice; and the Theodorian view that theft, sacrilege, and every kind of impurity are just in a sage, if he knows them to be of use to him. There is no help for it: I am in the same case as Alcibiades — I will never, if I can help it, put myself into the hands of a man who can decide on my head, where my life and honour will depend more on the skill and diligence of my attorney than on my own innocence. I would venture myself with the kind of justice that would take notice of my good deeds as well as my bad — where I had as much to hope as to fear. Acquittal is not enough pay for a man who has done better than merely not gone wrong. Our justice presents us with only one hand, and the left at that; whoever you are, you will come off with loss.

In China, whose government and arts, without any commerce with or knowledge of ours, surpass our examples in several outstanding features, and whose history teaches me how much greater and more various the world is than either the ancients or we have been able to grasp, the officers commissioned by the prince to visit the state of his provinces, while punishing those who behaved badly in their charge, also generously reward those who have conducted themselves better than the common run, beyond what duty required of them. These appear there not only to be approved but to gain; not simply to be paid, but to receive a gift.

No judge, thank God, has ever spoken to me in his capacity as a judge, on any account whatsoever, whether my own or anyone else's, criminal or civil; nor has any prison ever received me, not even to walk in. The very outside of a jail is unpleasant to my imagination; I am so in love with liberty that should I be forbidden access to some corner of the Indies I would live a little less at ease; and as long as I can find earth and air open elsewhere, I will never skulk in any place where I have to hide. My God, how badly would I bear the condition I see so many people in, nailed to a corner of the kingdom, deprived of the right to enter the principal cities and courts, and of the freedom of the public roads, because they have quarrelled with our laws. If those under which I live should so much as shake a finger at me in threat, I would immediately go look for others, wherever they might be. All my modest prudence in the civil wars in which we are now engaged is bent on this: that they should not hinder my liberty of going and coming.

Now, laws keep their credit not because they are just, but because they are laws; that is the mystical foundation of their authority, and they have no other — which serves their purpose well enough. They are often made by fools, more often by men who, out of hatred for equality, fail in equity, but always by men: vain and irresolute authors. Nothing is so grossly and ordinarily at fault as laws. Whoever obeys them because they are just does not justly obey them as he ought. Our French laws, by their irregularity and shapelessness, lend something of a helping hand to the disorder and corruption that show themselves in how they are dispensed and executed. The command is so tangled and inconstant that it in some way excuses both disobedience and shortcoming in interpreting, administering, and observing it. So whatever fruit we may pull from experience, that will little help our education if we draw it from foreign examples and make so little use of what we have at home — which is more familiar to us, and surely enough to teach us what we need. I study myself more than any other subject; it is my metaphysics, my physics:

"Quis deus hanc mundi temperet arte domum: / Qua venit exoriens, qua deficit: unde coactis / Cornibus in plenum menstrua luna redit / Unde salo superant venti, quid flamine captet / Eurus, et in nubes unde perennis aqua; / Sit ventura dies mundi quae subruat arces...."

["What god may govern with skill this dwelling of the world? Where does the monthly moon rise, where does she wane? How are her horns drawn together and opened again? Where do the winds prevail upon the sea? What does the east wind woo with its gusts? And where are the clouds perpetually supplied with water? Is a day to come which may bring down the world?" — Propertius, iii. 5, 26.]
"Quaerite, quos agitat mundi labor."
["Ask those whom the cares of the world trouble." — Lucan, i. 417.]

In this larger picture, I let myself be carried along ignorantly and carelessly by the general law of the world. I will know it well enough when I feel it; my learning cannot make it change course; it will not alter itself for me. It is folly to hope so, and a greater folly to fret about it, seeing that it is necessarily common to all and public. The goodness and capacity of the governor ought to absolve us of all care of the government; philosophical inquiries and contemplations serve no purpose except to feed our curiosity. With good reason the philosophers send us back to the rules of nature — but they have no business with so sublime a knowledge; they falsify those rules and present her face painted in too high and too adulterated a complexion, from which spring so many different pictures of one uniform subject. As she has given us feet to walk with, so she has given us prudence to guide us through life — not so ingenious, robust, and pompous a prudence as theirs, but one that is easy, quiet, and wholesome, and that performs quite well what the other only promises, in the man who is lucky enough to know how to put it to use sincerely and steadily — that is to say, according to nature. To commit oneself most simply to nature is to do it most wisely. Oh, what a soft, easy, and wholesome pillow ignorance and incuriosity make, on which to rest a well-ordered head!

I would rather understand myself well in myself than in Cicero. From the experience I have of myself I find enough to make me wise, if only I were a good student. Whoever calls to mind the excess of his past anger, and the degree to which that fever transported him, will see the deformity of the passion better than in Aristotle and conceive a more just hatred of it. Whoever remembers the ills he has gone through, those that have threatened him, and the slight occasions that have shifted him from one state to another, will by that prepare himself for future changes and for the knowledge of his condition. The life of Caesar has no greater example for us than our own; popular and commanding as it was, it is still a life subject to every human accident. Let us only listen: we will find in ourselves whatever we mostly need. Whoever calls to mind how many times he has been mistaken in his own judgment, is he not a great fool if he doesn't suspect it ever after? When another's reasoning convinces me of a false opinion of my own, I don't so much learn what new thing he said to me, or the particular ignorance involved — that would be small gain — as, in general, I learn my own weakness and the treachery of my understanding; and from that I draw the reform of the whole mass. In all my other errors I do the same, and I find great use in life from this rule: I don't look on the species or the individual as a stone I have stumbled over; I learn to suspect my footing throughout, and am careful to place my steps well. To learn that a man has said or done a foolish thing is nothing; a man must learn that he is nothing but a fool — a much more ample and important instruction. The false steps that my memory has so often taken, even when it was most sure and confident of itself, are not wasted on me; it swears and assures me in vain after the fact; I shake my ears at it; the first contradiction made to its testimony puts me in suspense, and I would not dare rely on it in anything of weight, nor warrant it in another person's affairs; and were it not that what I do for want of memory others do still more often for want of good faith, I would always, in a matter of fact, rather take the truth from another's mouth than from my own. If everyone would pry into the effects and circumstances of the passions that sway him, as I have done into those I am most subject to, he would see them coming, and would somewhat break their impetuosity and career. They do not always seize us suddenly; there are warnings, and there are degrees.
"Fluctus uti primo coepit cum albescere vento, / Paulatim sese tollit mare, et altius undas / Erigit, inde imo consurgit ad aethera fundo."
["As with the first wind the sea begins to whiten, then swells, then heaves higher and higher waves, until at last the ocean rises from its depths to the sky." — Aeneid, vii. 528.]

Judgment holds the chief seat in me; at least it carefully tries to. It leaves my appetites to take their own course — hatred and friendship, even the love I bear myself — without changing them or corrupting itself; if it cannot reform the other parts to its own model, at least it will not let itself be corrupted by them, but plays its game apart.

The advice given to everyone, "to know yourself," must be of important effect, since that god of wisdom and light had it written on the front of his temple as comprising everything he had to advise us. Plato says too that prudence is no other thing than the carrying out of this commandment; and Socrates verifies it in detail in Xenophon. The difficulties and obscurity of any science are not perceived except by those who are already inside it: a certain degree of understanding is needed to be able to know that a man does not know; we must push against a door to know whether it is locked against us. From which springs that Platonic subtlety, that "neither those who know are to inquire, since they know; nor those who do not know, since to inquire they must know what they are inquiring about." So in this matter of "knowing oneself," the fact that every man is seen so settled and satisfied with himself, that every man thinks himself sufficiently intelligent, shows that everyone knows nothing at all about it — as Socrates makes Euthydemus understand. I, who profess nothing else, find in it so infinite a depth and variety that all the fruit I have gathered from my learning serves only to make me feel how much I have still to learn. To my weakness, so often confessed, I owe the leaning I have toward modesty, to obedience to the belief prescribed to me, to a constant coldness and moderation of opinion, and to a hatred of that troublesome, wrangling arrogance, wholly believing and trusting in itself, which is the chief enemy of discipline and truth. Just listen to them lay down the law: the first foolish things they utter come in the very style with which men found religions and laws:
"Nihil est turpius, quam cognitioni et perceptioni assertionem approbationemque praecurrere."
["Nothing is more shameful than that assertion and approval should run ahead of knowledge and perception." — Cicero, Acad., i. 13.]

Aristarchus said that anciently scarcely seven sages could be found in the world, and in his own time scarcely so many fools. Have not we more reason than he to say so in this age of ours? Affirmation and obstinacy are express signs of want of wit. This fellow may have struck his nose against the ground a hundred times in one day, and yet he will be at his "therefores" as resolute and sturdy as before. You would say some new soul and vigour of understanding had been infused into him since, as happened to that ancient son of Earth, who took fresh courage and strength from his fall;
"Cui cum tetigere parentem, jam defecta vigent renovata robore membra:"
["Whose broken limbs, when they touched his mother earth, immediately gained new force." — Lucan, iv. 599.]

Does not this incorrigible blockhead think he assumes a new understanding by undertaking a new dispute? It is from my own experience that I accuse human ignorance, which is, in my opinion, the surest part of the world's school. Those who will not conclude as much in themselves, by so empty an example as mine or their own, let them believe it from Socrates, the master of masters; for the philosopher Antisthenes said to his disciples: "Let us go and hear Socrates; there I will be a pupil with you." And maintaining the Stoic doctrine that virtue was sufficient to make a life completely happy, having no need of anything else, he added — "except for the strength of Socrates."

That long attention I give to considering myself also fits me well enough to judge others; and there are few subjects on which I speak better or with better excuse. I happen very often to see and discern the qualities of my friends more exactly than they do themselves; I have astonished some by the accuracy of my description, and given them warning about themselves. By being accustomed from my infancy to contemplate my own life in those of others, I have acquired a studious complexion in this; and when I am once intent on it, I let few things about me — countenances, humours, conversations — that serve that purpose escape me. I study everything, both what I should avoid and what I should follow. So in my friends I discover by their effects their inward inclinations; not by sorting this infinite variety of so diverse and disconnected actions into certain species and chapters, and distributing my parcels and divisions distinctly under known heads and classes:
"Sed neque quam multae species, nec nomina quae sint, / Est numerus."
["But neither can we enumerate how many kinds there are, nor what their names." — Virgil, Georgics, ii. 103.]

The wise speak and deliver their thoughts more specifically, piece by piece; I, who see no further into things than use teaches me, present mine generally without rule and experimentally. I pronounce my opinion by disjointed articles, as something that cannot be spoken at once and as a whole; relation and conformity are not to be found in such low and common souls as ours. Wisdom is a solid and entire building, in which every piece keeps its place and bears its mark:
"Sola sapientia in se tota conversa est."
["Only wisdom is wholly turned upon itself." — Cicero, De Finibus, iii. 7.]

I leave it to the artists, and I don't know whether or not they will be able to bring it about — in so tangled, minute, and accidental a thing — to marshal into distinct bodies this infinite diversity of faces, to settle our inconstancy and set it in order. I find it hard not only to piece our actions to one another, but also to designate each of them properly by any single principal quality, so ambiguous and various are they when seen by different lights. What is remarked as rare in Perseus, king of Macedon, "that his mind, fixing itself to no one condition, wandered through every kind of living, and showed manners so wild and erratic that neither he himself nor anyone else knew what kind of man he was" — that seems to fit nearly all the world; and especially, I have seen another of his sort, to whom I think this conclusion fits even better: no moderate fixedness, but ever rushing headlong from one extreme to another on occasions not to be guessed at; no line of path without crosscurrent and astonishing contrariety; no single quality simple and unmixed; so that the best guess men can one day make about him will be that he affected and studied to make himself known by being not to be known. A man needs sound ears to hear himself frankly criticised; and since few can endure to hear it without being nettled, those who venture to do it for us show an uncommon effect of friendship; for it is to love sincerely indeed to dare to wound and offend us, for our own good. I find it hard to judge a man whose ill qualities are more than his good ones; Plato requires three things in him who would examine the soul of another: knowledge, goodwill, boldness.
I have sometimes been asked what I would have thought myself fit for, had anyone designed to make use of me, while I was of suitable years:
"Dum melior vires sanguis dabat, aemula necdum / Temporibus geminis canebat sparsa senectus:"
["While better blood gave me strength, and envious old age had not yet whitened my temples." — Aeneid, v. 415.]

— "For nothing," I said; and I willingly excuse myself from knowing anything that enslaves me to others. But I would have told my master the truth, and regulated his manners — if he had so pleased — not in a lump, by scholastic lessons, which I don't understand, and from which I see no real reformation arise in those who do; but by observing him at leisure, on every occasion, and simply and naturally judging them as an eyewitness, distinctly one by one; giving him to understand on what terms he stood in the common opinion, as against his flatterers. There is none of us who would not be worse than kings, if so continually corrupted as they are by that sort of rabble. How, if Alexander, that great king and philosopher, cannot defend himself against them!

I would have had fidelity, judgment, and freedom enough for the office. It would have to be a nameless office, otherwise it would lose its grace and its effect; and it is a part not equally fit for all men, for truth itself does not have the privilege of being spoken at all times and indifferently; its use, noble as it is, has its circumspections and limits. It often happens, as the world goes, that a man slips it into the ear of a prince not only to no purpose but injuriously and unjustly; and no one will make me believe that a virtuous remonstrance may not be viciously applied, and that the interest of the substance does not often have to give way to that of the form.
For such an office I would want a man content with his own fortune:
"Quod sit, esse velit, nihilque malit,"
["Who is pleased with what he is, and desires nothing more." — Martial, x. 47, 18.]

— and of moderate station, since on the one hand he would not be afraid to touch his master's heart to the quick, for fear of losing his preferment, and on the other hand, not being of high quality, he would have easier communication with people of every sort. I would have this office limited to one person only; for to grant the privilege of his liberty and privacy to many would breed an inconvenient irreverence; and of that one, above all things, I would require the fidelity of silence.

A king is not to be believed when he boasts of his constancy in standing up to the shock of the enemy for the sake of glory, if for his own profit and amendment he cannot stand the liberty of a friend's advice — which has no other power but to pinch his ear, the rest of its effect being still in his own hands. Now, there is no condition of men who stand in greater need of true and free advice and warning than they do; they bear a public life and have to satisfy the opinions of so many spectators; and as those around them conceal from them whatever would divert them from their own way, they find themselves, without noticing it, sunk in the hatred and detestation of their people, often on occasions they could have avoided without any prejudice even to their pleasures, had they been advised and corrected in time. Their favourites commonly have more regard for themselves than for their master; and it pays them, since in truth most offices of real friendship, when applied to a sovereign, are under rude and dangerous risk, so that they require not only very great affection and freedom, but courage too.

In short, all this hodgepodge that I scribble here is nothing but a record of the trials of my own life, which, on the side of inward soundness, is exemplary enough to take instruction against the grain. But as to bodily health, no one can furnish more profitable experience than I, who present it pure and in no way corrupted or changed by art or opinion. Experience is properly on its own dunghill in the subject of medicine, where reason wholly gives place to it. Tiberius said that whoever had lived twenty years ought to be answerable to himself for everything that was harmful or wholesome to him, and to know how to manage himself without doctors;

[All that Suetonius says in his Life of Tiberius is that this emperor, after he was thirty years old, governed his health without the aid of physicians; and what Plutarch tells us, in his essay on the Rules and Precepts of Health, is that Tiberius said that the man who, having attained sixty years, held out his pulse to a physician was a fool.]

And he might have learned it from Socrates, who, advising his disciples to be solicitous of their health as a chief study, added that it would be hard if a man of sense, looking after his exercise and diet, did not know better than any physician what was good or bad for him. And medicine itself professes always to have experience as the test of its operations: Plato had reason to say that to be a true physician, the man who would become one would first have to pass through all the diseases he proposes to cure, and through all the accidents and circumstances on which he is to judge. They might as well catch the pox, if they want to know how to cure it; for my part, I would put myself in such hands. The others only direct us like a man who paints seas and rocks and ports sitting at a table, where he makes the model of a ship sailing in all security; but put him to the work itself, and he doesn't know which end to begin at. They describe our maladies the way a town crier does a lost horse or dog — such a colour, such a height, such an ear — but bring it to him, and he doesn't recognise it for all that. If medicine should one day give me some good and visible relief, then truly I will cry out in good earnest:
"Tandem efficaci do manus scientiae."
["At last I yield my hands to an effective science." — Horace, Epod., xvii. 1.]

The arts that promise to keep our bodies and souls in health promise a great deal; but, for all that, none keeps its promise less. And in our time, those who profess these arts among us show the effects of them less than any other sort of men; at most one might say of them that they sell medicinal drugs, but that they are physicians a man cannot say.
[The edition of 1588 adds: "Judging by themselves, and those who are ruled by them."]

I have lived long enough to be able to give an account of the habits that have carried me this far; for anyone who has a mind to try it, I have done the tasting for him. Here are some of the items, as my memory supplies them; I have no habit that has not varied with circumstances, but I record only those I have known best and that have so far had the greatest possession of me.

My way of life is the same in sickness as in health; the same bed, the same hours, the same food, even the same drink, serve me alike in both conditions. I add nothing to them except the moderation of more or less, according to my strength and appetite. My health consists in keeping my usual state undisturbed. I see that sickness pushes me off it on one side, and if I let the physicians take charge, they will push me off on the other; so that between fortune and art I find myself driven from my proper path. I believe nothing more firmly than this: that I cannot be harmed by the use of things I have been so long accustomed to. It belongs to habit to give a form to a man's life, just as it pleases him; she is everything in that. She is Circe's potion, varying our nature however she pleases. How many nations only three steps from us think it a ridiculous fancy to fear the night dew, which is so obviously harmful to us, and our own watermen and peasants laugh at it. You make a German sick if you lay him on a mattress, an Italian if you lay him on a feather bed, a Frenchman if without curtains or fire. A Spanish stomach can't hold out to eat as we do, nor ours to drink like the Swiss. A German made me very merry at Augsburg by finding fault with our hearths, on the same grounds we usually use to run down their stoves; for to say the truth, the smothered heat, and then the smell of the heated matter the fire is made of, very much offend those not used to them — not me. The heat, being always even, constant, and universal, without flame, without smoke, and without the wind that comes down our chimneys, may in many ways stand comparison with ours. Why do we not imitate Roman architecture? They say that anciently fires were not made in the houses, but outside, at the foot of them, from where the heat was carried into the whole building by pipes contrived in the wall, winding around the rooms to be warmed — which I have seen plainly described somewhere in Seneca. This German, hearing me praise the conveniences and beauties of his city, which truly deserves it, began to pity me that I had to leave it, and the first inconvenience he urged on me was the heaviness of head that the chimneys elsewhere would give me. He had heard someone make this complaint and fixed it on us, being himself, by custom, unable to perceive it at home. All heat that comes from the fire weakens and dulls me. Evenus said that fire was the best seasoning of life: I would rather have any other way of warming myself.

We are afraid to drink our wine from near the bottom of the cask; in Portugal those fumes are reckoned delicious, and the beverage of princes. In short, every nation has many customs and usages that are not only unknown to other nations, but seem to them barbarous and miraculous. What are we to do with the people who admit no evidence that is not in print, who do not believe men if they are not in a book, nor truth if it is not of competent age? We dignify our follies when we commit them to the press: it weighs a great deal more to say, "I have read such a thing," than "I have heard such a thing." But I, who no more disbelieve a man's mouth than his pen, and who know that men write as indiscreetly as they speak, and who look on this age as one already past, am as ready to quote a friend as Aulus Gellius or Macrobius, and what I have seen as what they have written. And as it is held about virtue that it is not greater for having lasted longer, so I hold about truth that it is none the wiser for being older. I often say it is mere foolishness that makes us run after foreign and scholastic examples; their fertility is the same now as it was in the time of Homer and Plato. But isn't it that we look for more honour from the citation than from the truth of the thing in hand? As if it were more to the point to borrow our proofs from the bookshops of Vascosan or Plantin than from what is to be seen in our own village? Or rather, that we lack the wit to pick out and make useful what we see in front of us, and to judge it clearly enough to draw it into an example. For if we say we need authority to give credit to our testimony, we speak beside the point — since, in my opinion, out of the most ordinary, common, and known things, if we could but find their light, the greatest miracles of nature might be formed, and the most wonderful examples, especially on the subject of human actions.

Now, on this point, setting aside the examples I have gathered from books and what Aristotle says of Andron the Argive — that he travelled across the arid sands of Libya without drinking — a gentleman who has acquitted himself very well in several employments said in a place where I was that he had ridden from Madrid to Lisbon in the heat of summer with nothing to drink at all. He is very healthy and vigorous for his age, and has nothing extraordinary in his way of living except this, that he sometimes goes two or three months — even a whole year, he told me — without drinking. He is sometimes thirsty, but he lets it pass, and he holds that it is an appetite that easily wears itself out; and he drinks more out of caprice than out of need or pleasure.

Here is another example: it is not long ago that I found one of the most learned men in France, among those of not inconsiderable fortune, studying in a corner of a hall they had partitioned off for him with tapestry, with a rabble of his servants around him full of licence. He told me — and Seneca says almost the same of himself — that he made an advantage of this hubbub; that, beaten about by this noise, he so much the more collected and withdrew himself into himself for contemplation, and that this tempest of voices drove his thoughts back inward. Being a student at Padua, he had had his study for so long amid the rattle of coaches and the tumult of the square that he formed himself not only to a contempt of noise but even to a use of it, for the service of his studies. Socrates answered Alcibiades, who was astonished to know how he could endure the perpetual scolding of his wife: "Why," he said, "as those do who are accustomed to the ordinary noise of wheels drawing water." I am quite the opposite; my head is tender and easily put off balance; when it is bent on anything, the least buzzing of a fly murders it.

Seneca, in his youth, having warmly taken up the example of Sextius — eating nothing that had died — went a whole year without such food, and, as he says, with pleasure. He gave it up only so as not to be suspected of taking up the rule from some new religion that prescribed it. He adopted from Attalus, in the same way, the custom of not lying on any sort of bedding that gave way under his weight, and even into his old age made use of such as would not yield to any pressure. What the usage of his time made him reckon as roughness, that of ours makes us look on as effeminacy.

Just observe the difference between the way of life of my labourers and my own; the Scythians and Indians have nothing more remote both from my capacity and my form. I have taken in charity-boys to serve me, who soon after have quit both my kitchen and my livery only that they might go back to their former way of life; and I found one of them later picking mussels out of the sewer for his dinner — whom I could not, by entreaties or threats, reclaim from the sweetness he found in want. Beggars have their magnificences and delights, as well as the rich, and (so they say) their dignities and politics. These are the effects of habit; she can mould us not only into whatever form she pleases (the sages say we should apply ourselves to the best, which she will soon make easy for us), but also to change and variation, which is the most noble and most useful instruction she gives us. The best of my bodily conditions is that I am flexible and not very obstinate. I have inclinations more my own and ordinary, and more agreeable to me, than others; but I am diverted from them with very little ado, and easily slip into a contrary course. A young man ought to cross his own rules, to wake up his vigour and keep it from going faint and rusty; and there is no course of life so weak and dull as one that is conducted by rule and discipline;
"Ad primum lapidem vectari quum placet, hora / Sumitur ex libro; si prurit frictus ocelli / Angulus, inspecta genesi, collyria quaerit;"

["When he is pleased to be carried to the first milestone, the hour is chosen from the almanac; if he just rubs the corner of his eye, his horoscope is consulted, and he calls for salves." — Juvenal, vi. 576.]

Such a man should often throw himself into excesses, if he will take my advice; otherwise the slightest debauch will undo him, and make him troublesome and disagreeable in company. The worst quality in a well-bred man is over-fastidiousness and an attachment to a particular way of doing things; and it is particular, if it is not pliable and supple. It is a kind of reproach not to be able, or not to dare, to do what we see those around us do; let such men stay at home. It is unbecoming in any man, but in a soldier vicious and intolerable: a soldier, as Philopoemen said, ought to accustom himself to every variety and unevenness of life.

Though I have been brought up, as much as could be done, to liberty and independence, yet so it is that, growing old and having through indifference settled more into certain forms (my age is now past instruction, and has nothing further to do but to keep itself up as best it can), custom has already, without my noticing it, so imprinted its character in me in certain things that I look on it as a kind of excess to leave them off; and without forcing myself I cannot sleep in the daytime, nor eat between meals, nor breakfast, nor go to bed without a long interval between eating and sleeping — say three hours after supper; nor make children except before sleeping, nor make them standing; nor endure my own sweat; nor quench my thirst with pure water or pure wine; nor keep my head long bare; nor have my hair cut after dinner. I would be as uncomfortable without my gloves as without my shirt, or without washing when I rise from table or from bed; and I could not lie without a canopy and curtains, as if they were essential things. I could dine without a tablecloth, but without a clean napkin, in the German fashion, very uncomfortably; I dirty them more than the Germans or Italians do, and I make little use of either spoon or fork. I am sorry they didn't keep up the fashion, begun after the example of kings, of changing our napkin at every course, as they do our plate. We are told of that laborious soldier Marius that, growing old, he became nice in his drink, and never drank but out of a particular cup of his own; I, in the same way, have let myself fancy a certain form of glasses, and don't willingly drink in common glasses, any more than from a strange common hand; all metal offends me by comparison with a clear and transparent matter — let my eyes taste too, according to their capacity. I owe several other such niceties to habit. Nature has also, on the other side, helped me to some of hers: as not being able to endure more than two full meals in one day, without overcharging my stomach, nor a total abstinence from one of those meals without filling myself with wind, drying up my mouth, and dulling my appetite; the great inconvenience I find from too much evening air, for of late years, in night marches, which often happen to be all night long, after five or six hours my stomach begins to be queasy, with a violent pain in my head, so that I always vomit before day can break. When the others go to breakfast, I go to sleep; and when I get up, I am as brisk and gay as before. I had always been told that the night dew never rises but at the beginning of the night; but for some years past, by long and close company with a lord taken with the opinion that the night dew is sharper and more dangerous about the declining of the sun, an hour or two before it sets, which he carefully avoids — while despising that of the night — he has nearly imposed on me, not so much by his reasoning as by his experience. What? Shall mere doubt and inquiry strike our imagination so as to change us? Those who absolutely and suddenly give way to such inclinations bring total destruction on themselves. I am sorry for several gentlemen who, through the folly of their physicians, have in their youth and health shut themselves entirely up; better to put up with a cough than, by disuse, lose for ever the commerce of common life in things of such great use. Malignant science, to forbid us the most pleasant hours of the day! Let us keep our possession to the last. For the most part, a man hardens himself by being obstinate, and corrects his constitution, as Caesar did the falling sickness, by sheer contempt. A man should attach himself to the best rules, but not enslave himself to them — except such, if there are any, where obligation and servitude bring profit.

Kings and philosophers go to stool, and ladies too; public lives are bound to ceremony; mine, obscure and private, enjoys every natural dispensation. Soldier and Gascon are also qualities a little subject to indiscretion; so I shall say of this act of relieving nature that it is desirable to refer it to certain set and nocturnal hours, and to compel oneself to this by habit, as I have done; but not to subject oneself, as I have done in my declining years, to a particular convenience of place and seat for the purpose, and so make it troublesome by long sitting. And yet, in the fouler offices, isn't it in some measure excusable to require more care and cleanliness?
"Natura homo mundum et elegans animal est."
["Man is by nature a clean and refined creature." — Seneca, Epist., 92.]

Of all the actions of nature, I am the most impatient of being interrupted in that one. I have seen many soldiers troubled with the unruliness of their bowels; mine and I never fail of our punctual appointment, which is at jumping out of bed, if some indispensable business or sickness doesn't molest us.

I think then, as I said before, that sick people cannot put themselves anywhere in safer keeping than in staying still in the course of life in which they have been raised and trained; change, whatever it is, distempers and puts one out of step. Do you really believe chestnuts can hurt a Périgordian or a Lucchese, or that milk and cheese hurt the mountain people? We prescribe them not only a new but a contrary method of life — a change healthy people cannot bear. Prescribe water to a Breton of seventy; shut a sailor up in a stove; forbid a Basque footman to walk: you will deprive them of motion, and in the end of air and light.

"An vivere tanti est? / Cogimur a suetis animum suspendere rebus, / Atque, ut vivamus, vivere desinimus. . . . / Hos superesse reor, quibus et spirabilis aer / Et lux, qua regimur, redditur ipsa gravis."

["Is life worth so much? We are forced to withhold the mind from the things we are used to; and, that we may live, we cease to live. . . . Do I consider that they still live, to whom the breathable air, and the light itself by which we are governed, is made oppressive?" — Pseudo-Gallus, Eclog., i. 155, 247.]
If they do no other good, they do this at least: they prepare patients betimes for death, by little and little undermining and cutting off the use of life.

Both well and sick, I have always willingly let myself obey the appetites that pressed on me. I give a great deal of rein to my desires and inclinations; I do not love to cure one disease by another; I hate remedies more troublesome than the disease itself. To be subject to colic, and subject to abstain from eating oysters, is two evils instead of one — the disease torments us on the one side, the remedy on the other. Since we are always in danger of mistaking, let us at least take the chance of mistaking after we have had the pleasure. The world goes the opposite way and thinks nothing profitable that isn't painful; it is very suspicious of ease. My appetite, in various things, has of itself happily enough accommodated itself to the health of my stomach. Relish and pungency in sauces were pleasant to me when I was young; my stomach took a dislike to them later, and my taste followed at once. Wine is harmful to sick people, and is the first thing my mouth finds distasteful then, with a dislike I cannot get over. Whatever I take against my liking does me harm; and nothing hurts me that I eat with appetite and delight. I never had harm from any action that gave me real pleasure, and accordingly I have made all medical conclusions give way to my pleasure; and I have, when I was young,
"Quem circumcursans huc atque huc saepe Cupido / Fulgebat crocina splendidus in tunica."
["When Cupid, fluttering round me here and there, shone in his rich purple mantle." — Catullus, lxvi. 133.]
— given myself the rein as licentiously and inconsiderately to the desire that was uppermost in me as any other whatever:
"Et militavi non sine gloria;"
["And I have done my soldiering not without glory." — Horace, Od., iii. 26, 2.]
— yet more in continuation and stamina than in sudden sally:
"Sex me vix memini sustinuisse vices."
["I can scarcely remember holding out six bouts in one night." — Ovid, Amor., iii. 7, 26.]

It is at once a misfortune and a marvel to confess at what a tender age I first came under the subjection of love: it was indeed by chance, for it was long before the years of choice or knowledge; I do not remember myself that far back; and my fortune may well be coupled with that of Quartilla, who could not remember when she had been a maid.
"Inde tragus, celeresque pili, mirandaque matri / Barba meae."
["Thence the odour of the armpits, the precocious hair, and the beard that astonished my mother." — Martial, xi. 22, 7.]

Physicians bend their rules to the violent longings that come over sick people, ordinarily with good success; that great desire cannot be imagined so strange and vicious but that nature must have a hand in it. And then how easy a thing it is to satisfy the imagination! In my opinion, this part wholly carries it, at least over the rest. The most grievous and ordinary evils are those that imagination loads us with. This Spanish saying pleases me on several counts:
"Defenda me Dios de me."
["God defend me from myself."]

I am sorry when I am sick that I have no longing that might give me the pleasure of satisfying it; all the rules of medicine would hardly be able to divert me from it. I do the same when I am well; I can see very little more to be hoped for or wished for. It would be a pity for a man to be so weak and languishing as not to have even wishing left.

The art of medicine is not so fixed that we need lack authority for anything we choose to do; it changes with climates and moons, according to Fernel and to Scaliger. If your physician does not think it good for you to sleep, to drink wine, or to eat such-and-such meats, never trouble yourself; I will find you another who will not be of his opinion; the variety of medical arguments and opinions covers every sort and form. I saw a miserable sick man panting and burning for thirst — that he might be cured — who was afterward laughed at by another physician for his pains, this one condemning the advice as harmful to him. Hadn't he tormented himself to good purpose? There died lately of the stone a man of that profession who had used extreme abstinence to fight his disease; his fellow physicians say, on the contrary, that this abstinence had dried him up and baked the gravel in his kidneys.

I have observed that in both wounds and sicknesses, speaking discomposes and hurts me as much as any irregularity I can commit. My voice pains and tires me, for it is loud and forced; so that when I have gone to whisper to some great persons about affairs of consequence, they have often had to ask me to lower it.

This story is worth a digression. Someone in a certain Greek school, speaking loudly as I do, was sent by the master of ceremonies a message to speak softly. "Tell him then," the other replied, "that he must send me the tone he wants me to speak in." To which the message came back, "That he should take the tone from the ears of the man he is speaking to." Well said, if it is to be understood as "Speak according to the matter you are speaking about, and to your hearer"; for if it means, "Speak only loud enough for him to hear," or "Govern yourself by him," I do not find it reasonable. The tone and motion of my voice carry a great deal of the expression and meaning of what I say, and it is for me to govern them, to make myself understood: there is a voice to instruct, a voice to flatter, and a voice to rebuke. I want my voice not only to reach him but, if need be, to strike and pierce him. When I am chiding my valet with sharp, bitter language, it would be very pretty for him to say, "Please, master, speak lower, I hear you well enough":
"Est quaedam vox ad auditum accommodata, non magnitudine, sed proprietate."
["There is a certain voice fitted to the hearing, not by loudness but by propriety." — Quintilian, xi. 3.]

Speaking is half the speaker's and half the hearer's; the hearer must prepare himself to receive it according to its bent; just as with tennis players, the receiver shifts and prepares himself according to how he sees the striker move, and according to the stroke itself.
Experience has also taught me this: that we ruin ourselves by impatience. Evils have their life and their limits, their sicknesses and their recoveries.

The constitution of maladies is fashioned on the pattern of the constitution of animals; they have their fortune and their span of days set from their birth; the man who tries imperiously to cut them short by force, in the middle of their course, only lengthens and multiplies them, and inflames them instead of soothing them. I share Crantor's opinion that we are neither obstinately and deafly to resist our evils nor to give in to them out of want of courage, but to yield to them naturally, according to their condition and our own. We ought to grant a free passage to diseases; I find they stay less with me when I let them alone, and I have lost some of those reputed most tenacious and obstinate by their own decay, without help and without art, and contrary to its rules. Let us let nature take her course a little; she understands her own business better than we do. "But So-and-so died of it; and so shall you." If not of that disease, then of another. And how many have not escaped dying, who had three physicians at their heels? Example is a vague and universal mirror, with all sorts of reflections. If a medicine is delicious, take it: it is always so much present good. I will never stick at the name or the colour, if it is pleasant and grateful to the palate; pleasure is one of the chief kinds of profit. I have suffered colds, gouty defluxions, slack bowels, palpitations of the heart, migraines, and other things to grow old and die in time a natural death. I have lost them just when I was halfway resigned to keep them; they are sooner prevailed upon by courtesy than by bluster. We must patiently bear the laws of our condition: we are born to grow old, to grow weak, and to be sick, in spite of all medicine. It is the first lesson the Mexicans teach their children; as soon as ever they are born they thus salute them: "You have come into the world, child, to endure: endure, suffer, and say nothing." It is unjust to lament what befalls any one which may befall every one:
"Indignare, si quid in te inique proprio constitutum est."
["Be angry only when something is decreed unjustly against you alone." — Seneca, Epist., 91.]
See an old man begging God to maintain his health vigorous and entire — which is to say, to give him back his youth:
"Stulte, quid haec frustra votis puerilibus optas?"
["Fool, why do you vainly form these childish wishes?" — Ovid, Trist., iii. 8, 11.]

Is it not folly? His condition is not capable of it. Gout, stone, and indigestion are symptoms of long years, as heat, rain, and wind are of long journeys. Plato does not believe that Asclepius troubled himself by regimen to prolong life in a weak and wasted body, useless to its country and its profession, or to beget healthy and robust children; he doesn't think this care suitable to divine justice and prudence, which is to direct everything to its use. My good friend, your business is done: nobody can restore you; they can at most patch you up and prop you a little, and so prolong your misery for an hour or two:
"Non secus instantem cupiens fulcire ruinam, / Diversis contra nititur obicibus; / Donec certa dies, omni compage soluta, / Ipsum cum rebus subruat auxilium."

["Like one who, wishing to prop up an impending ruin, sets various supports against it, until at last, in a short time, the house, the supports, and all, giving way together, fall down at once." — Pseudo-Gallus, i. 171.]

We must learn to suffer what we cannot avoid; our life, like the harmony of the world, is made up of contraries — of various tones, sweet and harsh, sharp and flat, sprightly and solemn. What could the musician do who would only have some of these? He must know how to use them all, and mix them; and so we should mingle the goods and the evils that are consubstantial with our life. Our being cannot subsist without this mixture, and the one part is no less necessary to it than the other. To try to fight against natural necessity is to imitate Ctesiphon's folly, who set himself to kick with his mule.

I consult little about the alterations I feel in myself, for the doctors take advantage of you; once they have you at their mercy, they fill your ears with their prognostics. Formerly, surprising me when I was weakened by sickness, they handled me injuriously with their dogmas and magisterial follies — at one moment threatening me with great pains, at another with approaching death. I was indeed moved and shaken by this, but not subdued nor jostled out of my place; and though my judgment was neither altered nor distracted, it was at least disturbed: it is always agitation and combat.

Now, I treat my imagination as gently as I can, and would, if I could, discharge it of all trouble and contest; one must help, flatter, and deceive it if one can; my mind is fit for that office; it has no need of stage-effects throughout. If it could persuade as well as it preaches, it would relieve me successfully. Will you have an example? It tells me that "it is for my good to have the stone; that the structure of my age must naturally suffer some decay, and it is now time for it to begin to disjoin and to confess a breach; it is a common necessity, and there is nothing in it either miraculous or new. I am therein paying what is owed to old age, and I can expect no better bargain. Society ought to comfort me: I have fallen into the most common infirmity of my age. I see everywhere men tormented by the same disease, and am honoured by the fellowship, since men of the best quality are most often afflicted with it. It is a noble and dignified disease. Of those struck by it, few suffer with so little pain; they have the trouble of a strict diet and of daily taking nauseous potions, while I owe my better state purely to my good luck — for some ordinary broths of eringo or burst-wort that I took twice or thrice to oblige the ladies (who, with greater kindness than my pain was sharp, would have made me a present of half of theirs) seemed to me equally easy to take and useless in effect; while the others have to pay a thousand vows to Asclepius and as many crowns to their physicians for the voiding of a little gravel, which I often do by the aid of nature. Even the decorum of my countenance is not disturbed in company, and I can hold my water ten hours, and as long as any man in health. The fear of this disease," says my mind, "once terrified you when it was unknown to you; the cries and despairing groans of those who make it worse by their impatience bred a horror in you. It is an infirmity that punishes the members by which you have most offended. You are a man of conscience;"
"Quae venit indigne poena, dolenda venit:"
["It is right to complain of a punishment we have not deserved." — Ovid, Heroid., v. 8.]

"Consider this chastisement: it is very easy compared with others, and inflicted with paternal tenderness; just see how late it comes; it only seizes on and bothers the part of your life that is, one way or another, sterile and lost, as if by arrangement giving way to the licence and pleasures of your youth. The fear and the pity that people have of this disease serve you as material for glory — a quality the tincture of which your friends still detect in your complexion, even after your judgment has been purified and your reason has somewhat cured it. It is a pleasure to hear it said of yourself, 'What strength of mind! What patience!' You are seen sweating with pain, turning pale and red, trembling, vomiting blood, suffering strange contractions and convulsions, sometimes letting great tears fall from your eyes, urinating thick, black, and dreadful water, or having it suppressed by some sharp and ragged stone that cruelly pricks and tears the neck of the bladder — while all the while you entertain the company with an ordinary face; bantering by fits with your servants; taking your part in steady conversation; now and then excusing your pain, and making your suffering out to be less than it is. Do you remember the men of past times, who so eagerly sought out diseases to keep their virtue in breath and exercise? Put the case that nature is driving you and forcing you into this glorious school, into which you would never have entered of your own free will. If you tell me it is a dangerous and mortal disease, what other isn't? For it is a medical cheat to expect any that they say don't go straight to death: what matters it, if they go there by accident, or if they easily slide and slip into the road that leads to it? But you don't die because you are sick; you die because you are alive. Death kills you without needing the help of sickness; and sickness has put off death in some who have lived the longer because they thought themselves always dying. To which it may be added that, as in wounds, so in diseases, some are medicinal and wholesome. The stone is often no shorter-lived than you; we see men with whom it has lasted from infancy to extreme old age, and if they had not broken company with it, it would have been with them longer still; you more often kill it than it kills you. And even if it should present to you the image of approaching death, isn't that a good office to do a man of your age, to put him in mind of his end? And what is worse, you have nothing left that should make you desire to be cured. Whether or not, the common necessity will soon call you away. Just consider how cleverly and gently she puts you out of love with life, and weans you from the world; not forcing you with a tyrannical subjection, like so many other infirmities you see old men afflicted with, that hold them in continual torment and keep them in unbroken weakness and pain — but by warnings and lessons at intervals, broken up by long pauses of repose, as it were to give you opportunity to meditate and ruminate on your lesson at your own ease and leisure. To give you the means to judge rightly and to take the resolution of a man of courage, she shows you the state of your whole condition, both in good and evil — and on one and the same day a very cheerful and an unsupportable life. If you don't embrace death, at least you shake hands with it once a month; from which you have the more reason to hope that one day it will surprise you without warning; and that, having been so often led to the water's edge while still thinking yourself on the usual terms, you and your confidence will one day be unexpectedly ferried over. A man cannot reasonably complain of diseases that fairly divide the time with health."

I am obliged to Fortune for having so often assaulted me with the same sort of weapons; she forms and shapes me by habit, hardens and accustoms me, so that I now know within a little for how much I shall be quit. For want of natural memory, I make myself one on paper; and as any new symptom appears in my disease, I write it down, so that, having now passed through almost all sorts of examples, if anything striking threatens me, by turning over these little loose notes — as the Sibylline leaves — I never fail to find some matter of comfort from some favourable prognostic in my past experience. Habit also makes me hope better for the time to come; for the conduct of this clearing-out has held so long, it is to be supposed that nature will not change her course, and that no worse accident will happen than what I already feel. Besides, the condition of this disease is not unsuited to my prompt and sudden temperament; when it assaults me gently, I am afraid, for then it stays a great while; but it naturally has brisk and vigorous bouts; it claws me to purpose for a day or two. My kidneys held out an age without alteration; and I have now almost lived another since they changed their state. Evils have their periods, as well as benefits; perhaps the infirmity is drawing toward an end. Age weakens the heat of my stomach, and, its digestion being less perfect, sends this crude matter to my kidneys; why, at some turn, might not the heat of my kidneys also abate, so that they can no longer petrify my phlegm, and nature find out some other way of purgation? Years have plainly helped me to drain certain rheums; why not these excrements that supply the matter for gravel? But is there anything delightful in comparison of this sudden change, when from an excessive pain I come, by the voiding of a stone, to recover as by a flash of lightning the beautiful light of health, so free and so full, as happens in our sudden and sharpest colics? Is there anything in the pain suffered that one can set against the pleasure of so sudden a deliverance? Oh, how much more pleasant health seems to me after a sickness so near and so contiguous, that I can distinguish the two side by side at their greatest pitch, when they appear as if in emulation, as if to dispute the field one with the other! As the Stoics say that vices are usefully introduced to give value to virtue and set it off, we can with more reason and less rashness of conjecture say that nature has given us pain for the honour and service of pleasure and ease. When Socrates, after his fetters were knocked off, felt the pleasure of that itching the weight of them had caused in his legs, he rejoiced to consider the strict alliance between pain and pleasure, how they are linked together by a necessary connection, so that they follow each other by turns and beget one another; and he cried out to good Aesop that he should have taken from this consideration the matter for a fine fable.

The worst I see in other diseases is that they are not so grievous in their effect as they are in their wake: a man is a whole year recovering, full of weakness and fear all the while. There is so much hazard, and so many steps to take to reach safety, that there is no end of it; before they have unmuffled you of a kerchief, and then of a cap, before they let you walk abroad and take the air, drink wine, lie with your wife, eat melons, it is odds that you relapse into some new distemper. The stone has this privilege, that it carries itself clean off; whereas the other maladies always leave behind them some impression and alteration that makes the body liable to a new disease, and they lend a hand to one another. Those are excusable that content themselves with possessing us, without going further and bringing in their followers; but courteous and kind are those whose passage brings us some profitable issue. Since I have been troubled with the stone, I find myself freed from other accidents, much more, it seems to me, than I was before, and have never had any fever since. I reckon that the extreme and frequent vomitings to which I am subject purge me; and, on the other hand, my distastes for this and that, and the strange fasts I am forced to keep, digest my peccant humours, and nature, with these stones, voids whatever there is in me superfluous and hurtful. Let them not tell me that it is a medicine too dear bought; for what good are so many stinking draughts, so many caustics, incisions, sweats, setons, diets, and so many other methods of cure, which often, because we are unable to bear their violence and their pestering, bring us to our graves? So that when I have the stone, I look on it as medicine; when free of it, as an absolute deliverance.

And here is another particular benefit of my disease: that it almost plays its game by itself, and lets me play mine — if I have only courage to do it; for, in its greatest fury, I have endured it ten hours together on horseback. Just endure; you need no other regimen; play, run, dine, do this and that, if you can; your indulgence will do you more good than harm. Tell as much to one who has the pox, the gout, or hernia! Other diseases lay heavier obligations on us, rack our actions in a quite different way, disturb our whole order, and engage the whole state of life in their consideration; this one only pinches the skin; it leaves the understanding and the will wholly at our own disposal, and the tongue, the hands, and the feet; it wakes you up rather than dulls you. The soul is struck by the heat of a fever, overwhelmed by an epilepsy, displaced by a sharp migraine, and, in short, stunned by all the diseases that hurt the whole mass and its noblest parts; this one never meddles with the soul; if anything goes amiss with her, it is her own fault; she betrays, dismounts, and abandons herself. Only fools let themselves be persuaded that this hard, massive body baked in our kidneys can be dissolved by drinks; so once it has stirred, there is nothing to be done but give it passage; and it will make one for itself.

I observe this further particular convenience in it: that it is a disease in which we have little to guess at; we are spared the trouble that other diseases throw us into through the uncertainty of their causes, conditions, and progress, a trouble that is infinitely painful. We have no need of consultations and doctorly interpretations; the senses well enough inform us both what it is and where it is.

By such arguments, weak and strong — as Cicero with the disease of his old age — I try to rock my imagination to sleep and amuse it, and to dress its wounds. If I find them worse tomorrow, I will look for new stratagems. Take this for true: I have lately come to such a pass that the least motion forces pure blood out of my kidneys. So what? I move about, nevertheless, as before, and ride after my hounds with a juvenile and insolent ardour; and I hold that I have very good satisfaction for an accident of this importance, when it costs me no more than a dull heaviness and uneasiness in that part. There is some great stone wasting and consuming the substance of my kidneys and of my life, which I little by little evacuate, not without some natural pleasure, as an excrement henceforth superfluous and troublesome. Now if I feel anything stirring, don't fancy that I trouble myself to consult my pulse or my urine, in order to set myself on some annoying preventive course; I shall feel the pain soon enough, without making it more and longer by the disease of fear. He who fears he shall suffer already suffers what he fears. To which may be added that the doubts and ignorance of those who take it upon themselves to expound the designs of nature and her inward workings, and the many false prognostics of their art, ought to make us understand that her ways are inscrutable and utterly unknown; there is great uncertainty, variety, and obscurity in what she either promises or threatens. Except for old age, which is an undoubted sign of the approach of death, I see in all other events few signs of the future on which we can ground our divination. I judge of myself only by actual sensation, not by reasoning; to what end, since I am resolved to bring nothing to it but expectation and patience? Will you know what I gain by it? Look at those who do otherwise, and who rely on so many different persuasions and counsels; how often the imagination presses on them without any bodily pain.
